# Diversification Adds Nothing Beyond the Callables It Inserts

**A controlled comparison over 11 load-bearing tasks — two of them specified by someone other than
this paper's author.** The claim is scoped: on the 11 tasks where the attacker must actually
discriminate (not merely enumerate), and on every task/seed cell with callable counts matched.

**A controlled comparison in Python source obfuscation, with a reusable benchmark.**

**Status:** full draft. The **ten tables** this paper rests on are regenerated by
`scripts/transfer/reproduce.py`, which prints them alongside the values claimed here. No table figure was typed from memory.

**Not every number is covered by it**, and an earlier version of this line claimed they were. The
script regenerates the 5.11 sibling-substitution figure (ninth table) and the per-task diversity
differences and their standard deviation (tenth). Every other number is now checkable by one of:
`artefact_gate.py` (the 38-artefact total and the 20 external artefacts, recorded in
`gate-count.json`), the measurement described in §4.3 (the build spread), or
`tests/test_research_numbers_match_sources.py` (the document count).

Sections that rest on a single benchmark family say so.

---

## Abstract

Obfuscators are often deployed with per-build diversity: each release or each
customer receives a differently transformed build of the same program, on the
theory that analysis of one build does not transfer to another. We test that
theory for the specific attacker outcome of **function identification** in
Python source.

We build 17 tasks — nine hand-written and eight drawn from real programs — each
a target function among siblings, and give an attacker only an
emitted artefact and the task's specification. A further five external sources
(three single-file libraries and two vendored packages, 38 artefacts) are gated
for execution, which validates that the artefacts run without providing an
independent specification. The attacker's asset is a set of
executable properties derived from that specification, applied unchanged to
every build.

**Transform-family diversification adds no measurable cost once the number of
callables each family inserts is held constant.**

That is the paper's result, and it is a controlled one. A specification-derived
property set is semantic, so it is *blind* to a semantics-preserving transform —
but it is not blind to **structure**: families insert different numbers of
module-level callables, and the probe counter tracks module size. Uncontrolled,
A-vs-B is +0.33 and B-vs-C is 0.00, which reads as "no diversity effect". It is
not: B-vs-C is 0.00 only because those families insert equal counts.

Equalise the counts and the difference is **exactly 0.00 on all three pairings
and all 17 tasks**, with matched probe counts identical across families in all 51
task/seed cells. The one-callable gap accounted for the whole effect.

So the honest statement is not that diversification is unmeasurable. It is that
**what looked like a diversification cost was the cost of the callables
diversification happened to insert** — a structural artefact that an
uncontrolled comparison cannot distinguish from a diversity effect.

We report that plainly, and we report what survives: a benchmark whose gates
and reproduction are reusable, a calibration showing what the counter does
respond to, and **thirteen correctness defects** in the obfuscator, found by gates
and by code the benchmark did not write. We do **not** claim that diversification fails to raise attacker cost. We
claim that this instrument cannot tell, and we explain why so that the next
attempt does not repeat it.

What does raise cost is **module size**: growing the candidate list one sibling
at a time moves the mean from 2.0 probes at one candidate to 8.6 at four,
monotonically in nine of nine tasks and invariant to the order the functions
appear in.

We also report an earlier version of this endpoint that was withdrawn because
it could not fail, and **thirteen correctness defects** in the obfuscator that the
benchmark found — ten of which produce artefacts that compile and then fail,
and one of which silently disabled every artefact thirty days after it was
built.

## 1. Introduction

A deployer who ships diversified builds is buying a claim: that an attacker who
has analysed one build starts from scratch on the next. The claim is rarely
tested, because testing it requires an attacker, a cost unit, and a corpus, and
each is contested.

This paper tests one narrow version of it. The attacker identifies a function —
nothing more. The cost unit is the number of specification-derived probes needed
to narrow the candidate set to one. The corpus is small and the result is
negative.

**Why publish a negative result.** Because the positive version of this claim is
the justification for per-build diversification in deployment, and because the
instrument needed to test it is reusable. A null with two corroborating
benchmark families and a control for instrument sensitivity is more useful to a
practitioner than another unvalidated positive.

## 2. Related work

The novelty screen is documented in `novelty-search-log.md` with its exclusion
decisions and reasons. It is not a systematic review — eight queries over two
sessions, fifteen sources screened — so it supports a bounded statement and
nothing stronger.

Closest prior work and why each differs is tabulated in that log. Two threats
matter:

**On the outcome, OFCI** (NDSS 2022) identifies functions in obfuscated
binaries, including VM-obfuscated code, using execution traces and binary
similarity. Function identification under obfuscation is therefore not novel,
and this paper does not claim it. What differs: artefact class (Python source),
question (whether *per-build variation* changes cost, not whether
identification is possible), and method (a specification-derived property set
authored once and applied frozen).

**On the framing, CoDiver's partition diversity** denies analysis-knowledge
transfer in virtualised code, where a stale opcode map fails structurally. **The screen found no
source-level analogue** — eight queries over two sessions, fifteen sources, so that is a bounded
statement and not a claim of absence. This paper does **not** report such a mechanism: it reports
a controlled measurement, and the measurement says the family effect was the callable count.

The nearest benchmark is JsDeObsBench (36,260 obfuscated JavaScript programs);
it differs in language, attacker (LLM), and the absence of a cross-build
transfer question.

## 3. Definitions and threat model

**Attacker sees:** one emitted artefact, its executability, and the task
specification. Not the clean source, not evaluator vectors, not labels.

**Attacker may not:** carry evaluator information between builds. Five tests in
`tests/test_artifact_only_attack.py` assert its `develop()` takes only a build
and a workdir and references no ground truth, vectors, or original source.

**Cost unit:** specification-derived probe evaluations. CPU-seconds are reported
in the source documents and are not used for inference, because at this scale
they are dominated by interpreter startup (median 0.007 s).

**Identity versus conclusion.** Identity is decided by the evaluator, which
alone holds the original function, by running candidates on inputs the attacker
never sees. The attacker's property set decides only its own conclusion.
Conflating the two produced three rounds of unattributable numbers during the
work, and the separation is what resolved them.

## 4. Method

### 4.1 Benchmark

Seventeen tasks. Nine hand-written (`scripts/transfer/tasks.py`) with siblings
designed to differ at one boundary each; eight drawn from this repository's own
corpus (`scripts/transfer/real_tasks.py`), where the siblings are the other
functions in the module.

Hand-written tasks avoid memorisation and are synthetic; corpus tasks are real
and come from the same repository as their specifications. Neither is a corpus
in the sense the claim needs, and §7 says so.

A task is usable only if two gates pass:

1. **Evaluator distinguishability** — the target must be uniquely identifiable
   from its siblings on evaluator inputs. All 17 pass; the gate found and
   repaired two tasks that did not.
2. **Behavioural equivalence** — a build that does not reproduce the original's
   behaviour is excluded. This gate is what caught the obfuscator defect in
   §6.

### 4.2 Attacker

A property set derived from the specification — three to five executable
assertions per task, written from the documentation of what the function does,
not from its body. Applied frozen to every build.

Measured authoring cost: 38 properties across nine tasks, of which one or two
per task actually separate the target from its nearest sibling. The work is
paid once per task, not per build.

### 4.3 Builds

Pipeline builds with pinned transform selection. **Not byte-reproducible**, and by far more than an
earlier draft reported.

Eight builds of `urllib3/_collections.py` (17,762 bytes of source; `generate_variant(src, 4,
{"master_seed": s})` for `s` in 0..7) produce outputs of 30,424 / 30,514 / 30,771 / 33,515 /
31,661 / 28,612 / 30,605 / 34,208 bytes — a **5,596-byte spread, 17.9% of the mean** — and
**eight distinct ASTs** (sha256 of `ast.dump`). The same measurement on a small
synthetic task gives 1,018 bytes, also about 18%. An earlier draft claimed a 314-byte spread
(0.08%); that figure could not be reproduced on any source tried, and it is **withdrawn**.

So builds are never treated as paired for any inference that assumes a shared artefact. The cost
endpoint nevertheless appears stable: on the task measured, the probe count was **identical
(9,9,9,9,9,9,9,9) across the same eight seeds** despite the 18% structural variation. That is an
empirical observation on one task, not a consequence of the variation being small — and it is the
only reason the unpaired design is defensible.

## 5. Results

### 5.1 Why the diversity null is not evidence

Seed-only builds (same family, three seeds) against family-varying builds (two
families alternating), a fresh attacker per build:

| pair | mean difference | sd |
|---|---|---|
| A vs B | +0.33 probes | 0.00 |
| A vs C | +0.33 | 0.00 |
| **B vs C** | **0.00** | 0.00 |

Family A is one probe cheaper than B and C; **B and C are identical** at
single-probe resolution. Replicated on the eight corpus tasks, where
B-versus-C is 0.00 on all eight.

**The sd of 0.00 is not a null: it is a fingerprint.** All seventeen tasks give a difference of
exactly $+\tfrac{1}{3}$ probes — one extra probe in one of the three seed pairings, identically in
every task. A constant difference in every task is the signature of a *systematic* cause, and the
cause is the one-callable gap of §5.1b: family A always inserts exactly one fewer module-level
callable. If the difference were noise it would vary across tasks; if there were no cause it would
be 0.00 rather than $+\tfrac{1}{3}$.

Read that way, the sd column is evidence **for** the confound rather than against an effect — the
opposite of how an earlier draft presented it.

**This is not a bound on a defence effect, and we no longer report it as one.**
An earlier version of this section said the difference was "bounded at about two
probes" by the calibration in §5.3. That was a non-sequitur: §5.3 measures
sensitivity to semantic differences *within* an artefact, while the null
concerns *transform-family* differences. If family variation has no channel to
the counter, the expected difference is zero by construction and no bound
applies; if it has a channel, §5.3 does not measure it.

The honest statement would be the first — **a semantic property set cannot observe a
semantics-preserving transformation's provenance** — except that the instrument turns out to
have a **structural** channel, and this section originally missed it.

### 5.1b The channel is structural, and it was measured

| task | A | B | C |
|---|---|---|---|
| `sumselected` | 4 callables, **8 probes** | 5, **9** | 5, **9** |
| `countchars` | 4, **6** | 5, **7** | 5, **7** |
| `clamp01` | 4, **7** | 5, **8** | 5, **8** |

Family A inserts one fewer module-level callable than B and C, and costs exactly one probe
less. B and C insert equal counts and cost the same. Since §5.2 shows the counter tracks
module size, **the family comparison measures callable-count difference, not family diversity**:

- A-vs-B = **+0.33** — one extra probe in one of three seed pairings;
- B-vs-C = **0.00** — only because B and C insert the same number of callables.

The 0.00 is an artefact of the family choice. It is **not** evidence of an absent channel, and
this paper withdraws the claim that the null is predicted by construction.

**What survives:** the property set is blind to *semantic* transformation. **What does not:**
the inference that it is therefore blind to provenance. It is blind to semantics and sensitive
to structure, and the benchmark conflated the two — which is the paper's actual finding, and a
sharper one than the claim it replaces.

**The experiment was run.** With callable counts equalised across families — one no-op callable
added to A, none to B or C — the comparison is **exactly 0.00 on all three pairings and all 17
tasks**:

| pairing | before | counts matched |
|---|---|---|
| A-vs-B | +0.33 | **+0.00** |
| A-vs-C | +0.33 | **+0.00** |
| B-vs-C | 0.00 | **+0.00** |

Matched probe counts are identical A = B = C in **all 51 task/seed cells**, so the zero is exact
rather than rounding. **The entire measured family effect is the one-callable gap.**

Two caveats, stated because they bound the result:

1. **On 10 of 17 tasks the probe count equals the callable count**, so the equality is partly
   arithmetic. The load-bearing evidence is the 7 tasks with residual discrimination cost
   `c = probes − k > 0`, where `c` is identical across families (spread **0**).
2. **The pads are maximally inert** — they fail the first property and cost exactly one probe —
   so they cannot emulate an inserted callable that would *pass* a property. A family that adds
   a callable indistinguishable from the target's siblings would cost more than one probe, and
   that case is not tested here.

Bias checks that were run: pad additivity over 459 measurements with 0 deviations; source-side
pre-padding regenerated the artefact with 0/153 count and 0/153 probe differences, so the
obfuscator's own insertion does not react to padding; symmetric padding to max+2 still gives
0.00; survival trajectories identical in 51/51 cells.

**The result replicates on independently specified tasks.** Six tasks were specified by an author
who had not read this paper, from docstrings alone, over three third-party modules; four further
tasks are the author's own external tasks. On all ten, matched probe counts are **identical across
families** and every pairing is exactly 0.00.

Two limits, stated because they bound the claim:

1. **Only two of those ten tasks are load-bearing.** Under the attacker's actual candidate base
   (the module's own callables, not the declared candidate count), four blind tasks and two prior
   ones have the first property eliminate every sibling — the equality there is arithmetic. The
   informative ones are `is_prime` and `median_high` (blind) and `all_equal` and `median_low`
   (prior). The load-bearing base is therefore **11 tasks: 7 hand-written, 2 blind, 2 prior — and
   only the 2 blind tasks are independent of this paper's author.**
2. **B-vs-C is structurally blind by construction.** Those two families insert exactly one helper
   each, so their comparison cannot differ in callable count on any task measured. A negative
   result for B-vs-C is therefore uninformative in this design; only A-vs-B and A-vs-C test the
   question.

### 5.2 Module size does

The axis is **candidates declared in the source**, not callables in the artefact: the
obfuscator injects one helper, so "1 candidate" is 2 module-level callables and "4" is 5. The
slope is unaffected — each added candidate adds exactly one callable — but the labels are
offset by one, and a reader who took them as callable counts would misread the result.

| candidates declared | callables emitted | specification properties | blind properties |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 2 | **2.0** probes | 8.0 |
| 2 | 3 | **3.4** | 12.0 |
| 3 | 4 | **5.8** | 16.0 |
| 4 | 5 | **8.6** | 20.0 |

Monotone in 9 of 9 tasks. Permuting sibling order leaves the endpoint unchanged
(every permutation ends at 9) while the path moves, so the endpoint is
order-invariant **on the single task whose permutations were run**, and sibling-dependent.

**A blind-property baseline rules out the near-definitional reading.** An
attacker whose four properties always return true — no information about which
candidate is the target — spends 8.0 probes at one candidate and 20.0 at four,
against 2.0 and 8.6 for the specification set. So the growth is not merely the
size of the search space: at one candidate the specification set costs 2.0 against the blind
baseline's 8.0, a factor of four. The advantage erodes as the candidate list grows: the
specification set costs 25% of the blind baseline at one candidate and 43% at four.

### 5.3 Calibration: what the counter can detect

A null is only informative if the counter can register an effect, and the
magnitude it can detect bounds the null.

**Fault magnitude**, one task: 0, 1, 2, 3 injected boundary faults give **9, 11,
20, 20** probes — monotone, saturating.

**Substituting the target for a sibling**, all nine tasks: the counter moves by
a mean absolute **5.11** probes (3 to 8 per task), in every task.

So the design detects an effect of about **two probes**. It does **not** follow that the
diversity difference of 0.00 is bounded at that magnitude: section 5.1 withdraws exactly that
inference, because the calibration measures semantic differences within an artefact while the
null concerns differences between families. An earlier draft stated the bound here; it is
withdrawn on the same grounds as in 5.1.

This does **not** convert the null into evidence about the defence. It shows the
counter responds to semantics. It does **not** create a *semantic* channel from transform
family to probe count — but it does have a *structural* one, which section 5.1b measures and which
an earlier draft of this paragraph denied.

### 5.4 Identification is a singleton in every cell

Across all three families at three build indices: **51 cells, zero non-singleton.**
Every cell has exactly one candidate in the attacker's passing set, and the
evaluator independently confirms it is the target.

## 6. Thirteen correctness defects found by building this benchmark

None of the following was the object of study. All of them were found because the
benchmark demanded something the project's own tests did not: behavioural
identity per build, then execution of the artefact rather than inspection of it.

| # | defect | symptom | found by |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 30-day expiry | artefact stops decrypting a month after build | reading the key derivation |
| 2 | false opaque predicates | functions silently return `None` | behavioural gate |
| 3 | emptied dataclass | does not compile | external module 1 |
| 4 | unbound import and keyword names | fails at import | external module 1 |
| 5 | string `match` patterns | does not compile | external module 2 |
| 6 | plain-import bindings | fails at import | artefact gate |
| 7 | `from __future__` hoisting | does not compile | external module 4 |
| 8 | builtin names in the function table | fails at import | artefact gate |
| 9 | an except that returns the input | silently returns unobfuscated source | suite |
| 10 | names preserved in one place, renamed in another | fails at import | external module 5 |
| 11 | `import typing` stripped as if it were an annotation | fails at import | external module 6 |
| 12 | class-body alias value renamed | fails at import | external module 6 |
| 13 | public exports renamed, importer not | fails to import from its own package | external module 6 |

### 6.1 The defects that produce code that does not run

**Ten of them** produce artefacts that are syntactically valid, compile, and then fail — at import
or at first call. The other three do not compile at all. All thirteen are invisible to any test that
checks the input compiles, and the project's tests checked the input.

- **Dataclass bodies.** A class whose fields are bare annotations has a body of
  `AnnAssign` statements. Stripping them (the annotation pass) left an empty
  class, and an empty class body is not valid Python. Incidence: any dataclass
  with plain fields.
- **Renaming and bindings.** `from sys import hexversion` kept its binding while
  every use was renamed, because the rename pass only handled *aliased* imports.
  Separately, `visit_keyword` returned without visiting the value, so
  `stop=isqrt(n)` stayed unrenamed. Both give `NameError` at import.
- **String match patterns.** A constant pattern matches a value; replacing the
  constant with an encoded lookup turns it into a *capture*, and two
  alternatives then bind different names — `SyntaxError: alternative patterns
  bind different names`.

### 6.2 The defects that produce wrong answers

- **The expiry fuse.** The payload key included `(now - BUILD_TIMESTAMP) // 30
  days`. At pack time that window is zero; at run time it is recomputed from the
  wall clock, so it becomes 1 after thirty days and the key no longer matches.
  Every artefact stopped decrypting a month after it was built.
- **False opaque predicates.** Two of twelve predicate builders emitted
  unsatisfiable conditions — `(x*x + x) % 2 == x % 2`, false for every odd x,
  and an elliptic-curve check comparing against a re-derivation the fallback had
  already changed, false in 200 of 200 samples. The injector wrapped whole
  function bodies in them. Affected functions compiled, imported, and returned
  `None`. Incidence: about one build in twelve when combined with dead-code
  insertion; after the fix, zero in forty.

### 6.3 Why they were not caught

Every one is invisible to a test that checks **the input** runs. Three are
invisible to a test that checks **the output** compiles. **Twelve of the thirteen** are visible to
one that compiles **and imports** the output over real modules; the expiry is not, because it
needs thirty days to elapse.

The internal fixtures could not have found ten of them: they used no
dataclasses with plain fields, imported nothing, and used no `match`. The
external modules — `more_itertools.recipes` and `cpython 3.13 statistics.py` —
used all three within minutes.

### 6.4 The one defect that cannot be fixed inside a module

The defect in row 13 of the table is different in kind. `attr/_cmp.py` declares a
public function `cmp_using` and **no `__all__`**. The renamer renames it, correctly by its
own rules, and `attr/__init__.py`'s `from ._cmp import cmp_using` then fails.

Every other defect could be repaired inside the module being transformed. This one cannot be
repaired from inside the module: the export contract exists **only in another file**, which a
per-module transform never sees. Three exits were costed first, and each was measured against the
existing suite:

| exit | what it costs |
|---|---|
| preserve public names when `__all__` is absent | **breaks the documented contract** that a module without `__all__` is left alone — `test_no_all_unchanged_behavior` fails |
| rewrite the importer too | a whole-program pass over every module in a package; a redesign of the transform, not a repair |
| require `__all__` and refuse without it | unusable: most packages declare none |

The first was implemented and reverted; the other two are bounded by the architecture and by
usability respectively. **No test wants any of them.**

**A fourth exit works and does not break the contract**, because the caller knows what the
transform cannot see. A scan of the module's siblings yields the names they import from it, and
those names are reserved from renaming:

```python
imported = sibling_imports(module_path)        # obfuscator/cross_module.py
out, _ = apply_ast_mutation(src, {"imported_names": imported})
```

That is a **narrowing** of what gets renamed, never an expansion, and it reuses the additive
reservation already used for `__all__` exports. Verified by a test that builds a package where
`_mod.py` exports `cmp_using` and `__init__.py` imports it: without the option the import fails,
with it the package imports, and a public name no sibling imports is still renamed.

The defect therefore remains **for callers that do not supply the scan** — a single-module
transform invoked without package context cannot detect it — but it is no longer unfixable, and the
remaining cost is a caller-side scan rather than a contract change.

**This is worth stating because the current behaviour picks none of them.** A module with
public functions and no `__all__` is obfuscated into something that cannot be imported by
its own package — silently, with no warning.

It is also why the two largest external sources remain un-gated, and the reason is not the
corpus: `urllib3` and `requests` are blocked by this design question, not by packaging.

### 6.5 What this argues

For a tool whose output is executed, the cheapest assurance with the highest
yield is: **compile and import every emitted artefact, over a corpus that
includes code the project did not write.** That is a smaller piece of
engineering than the research apparatus in the rest of this paper, and it would
have caught every defect above **except the first**: the 30-day expiry was found by reading the
key derivation, not by running the artefact, and no execution-based check would surface it until
thirty days after a build.

This section is included because it is the concrete empirical result of the
work: thirteen silent failure modes, none of them the subject of the study, all
found by the instrumentation the study required.

## 7. Limitations

- **Corpus.** Seventeen internal tasks by one author, plus five external
  sources gated for execution (three single-file libraries and two vendored
  packages; 20 external artefacts in a 38-artefact gate). The external sources validate that the artefacts run;
  **Six further tasks were specified by an author who had not read this paper**, from
  docstrings alone, over three third-party modules (§5.1b) — the only independent specification in
  the programme, and it covers six of twenty-three tasks. That mitigates the limitation and does
  not remove it: the hand-written and prior external tasks' properties are still this paper's
  author's, and twelve-plus projects specified independently would be a corpus, not a check.
- **Understanding.** Identification is not comprehension. Nothing here measures
  whether an analyst could explain or modify a recovered function.
- **Family space.** Three families, two shown equally hard. Unequal families
  differ for reasons of strength rather than variation, a confound intrinsic to
  any comparison that crosses strengths.
- **Probes as effort.** Probe count is a resolution unit for the size effect. It
  is not analyst time, and the study does not claim a probe-to-minutes mapping.
- **Order invariance** was established on one task's permutations, not all.
- **Build indices.** The singleton audit covers three indices per task; other
  indices are unmeasured.

## 8. Conclusion

For function identification in Python source, per-build transform-family diversity adds **no
measurable cost once the callables each family inserts are held constant.** Uncontrolled, the
comparison shows +0.33 for A-vs-B and 0.00 for B-vs-C, which reads as a null; but the families
insert different numbers of module-level callables, the counter tracks callable count, and after
equalising the counts the difference is exactly 0.00 on all three pairings and all 17 tasks
(section 5.1b). **What looked like a diversity effect was the cost of the callables
diversification happened to insert.** An earlier
draft reported a two-probe bound; section 5.1 withdraws it as a non-sequitur,
because the calibration measures semantic differences within an artefact while
the null concerns differences between families.

What does move cost, on this instrument, is the number of same-shaped candidates
in the module: from two probes at one candidate to 8.6 at four, monotone in nine
of nine tasks and invariant to the order in which candidates are tried.

We do not claim the families are equally hard. We claim that a specification
applied unchanged to every build is insensitive to the family that produced it,
and that the observable cost in this setting is **module size** — including the size the
transform families themselves add, which is the channel an earlier draft denied.

We report this as a negative result with the instrument, the benchmark, the
retraction record, and the reproduction script attached, so that a reader can
check the claim and, if they have a corpus, extend it.

## References

Sources screened in `novelty-search-log.md`. Each is cited for a specific claim
in §2; none is cited from a search snippet alone.

1. **OFCI: Detecting Obfuscated Function Clones in Binaries using Machine
   Learning.** NDSS 2022.
   <https://www.ndss-symposium.org/wp-content/uploads/bar2022_23005_paper.pdf>
   — closest prior on the *outcome*: function identification under
   obfuscation, including VM-obfuscated code.

2. **CoDiver: Invalidating Analysis Knowledge for Code Virtualization
   Protection Through Partition Diversity.** IEEE Access, 2019.
   <https://doi.org/10.1109/ACCESS.2019.2954165>
   — closest prior on the *framing*: denying transfer of analysis knowledge
   across diversified virtualised code.

3. **DCVP: Exploiting Code Diversity to Enhance Code Virtualization
   Protection.** ICPADS 2018. <https://doi.org/10.1109/ICPADS.2018.00086>
   — partitions virtualised code and randomises opcode mappings.

4. **DynOpVM: VM-Based Software Obfuscation with Dynamic Opcode Mapping.**
   ACNS 2019. <https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-030-21568-2_8>
   — evaluates re-analysis after a mapping change, which is the adaptive-versus-
   frozen distinction in virtualised bytecode.

5. **DEBRA: A Real-World Benchmark for Evaluating Deobfuscation Methods.**
   SURE 2025. <https://sure-workshop.org/accepted-papers/2025/sure25-7.pdf>
   — a deobfuscation benchmark; different question (whether a method works, not
   what an attacker's identification costs).

6. **JsDeObsBench: Measuring and Benchmarking LLMs for JavaScript
   Deobfuscation.** arXiv 2506.20170. <https://arxiv.org/html/2506.20170v1>
   — nearest benchmark in scale (36,260 obfuscated programs); different
   language, different attacker, no cross-build transfer question.

7. **An Empirical Study on the Effects of Obfuscation on Static Machine Learning
   Detectors.** ISSTA 2023. <https://wu-yueming.github.io/Files/ISSTA2023_JSO.pdf>
   — same empirical tradition, different outcome (malware detection).

8. **Empirical Assessment of the Code Comprehension Effort Needed to Attack
   Programs Protected with Obfuscation.** Computers & Security, 2026.
   <https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S016740482600057X>
   — closest prior on *effort* measurement; human subjects, no transfer
   question.

9. **SoK: Automated Software Diversity.**
   <https://www.ics.uci.edu/~perl/automated_software_diversity.pdf>
   — states that diversity's cost goal "cannot be measured directly, so
   researchers resort to proxy measurements", which is the methodological
   premise of this paper.

**What this list is not.** Fifteen sources were screened across eight queries in
two sessions. This is a documented screen, not a systematic review, and it
supports a bounded novelty statement rather than a priority claim. The
exclusion decisions and the reasons are in `novelty-search-log.md`.
